title: Repeating Decimal as Text
statement:
You get two integers, num and den (never zero). Return the value of num / den written as a decimal string.

  • If the division is exact, write just the integer, like "6", with no decimal point.
  • If the digits after the point end, write them all, like "-2.25".
  • If they repeat forever, write the part before the repeat, then the shortest repeating block in parentheses, starting as early as possible: "0.58(3)", not "0.583(3)" or "0.58(33)".
  • A negative result starts with -. Zero is written "0", never "-0".

examples.why: 7/12 = 0.58333…; the 5 and 8 appear once and only the 3 repeats.
The digits end, so there are no parentheses. The sign comes from the signs of both inputs.
The remainder returns to its starting value after 6 digits, so all six repeat as one block.

constraints: The answer is at most 10 000 characters long
hints: Do long division by hand on 1/7 and watch the remainders. When do the digits start repeating?
Each digit depends only on the current remainder, and there are fewer than |den| possible remainders. The moment a remainder comes back, the digits from its first appearance on will repeat.
Store each remainder with the position of the digit it produced. When you see one again, insert '(' at the stored position and append ')'.

explain.intuition:
Long division produces one digit at a time from the current remainder: multiply it by 10, divide by den for the next digit, keep what is left over. The next step depends only on that remainder. So if a remainder you have seen before shows up again, everything since then will happen again, forever.

Remember where each remainder first appeared. The first repeat tells you exactly where the repeating block starts and that it ends just before now. If the remainder reaches 0 instead, the decimal stops. The sign and the integer part are handled once at the start on absolute values.
steps: If num is 0, return "0". Otherwise start with "-" if exactly one of the inputs is negative, and work with absolute values.
Append the integer part ⌊n / d⌋. If the remainder is 0, you are done; otherwise append ".".
While the remainder is not 0: if it is in the map, insert "(" at its stored position, append ")" and stop.
Otherwise store remainder → current length, multiply it by 10, append the next digit ⌊rem / d⌋ and keep rem mod d.
pitfalls: Taking the absolute value of −2³¹ in a 32-bit integer type. It overflows; use a 64-bit type (JavaScript numbers are fine).
Detecting the repeat by a repeated digit instead of a repeated remainder. In 1/333 the digit 0 repeats right away, but the block is 003.
Getting the sign from num only, or printing "-0" for a zero numerator with a negative denominator.

complexity.time: O(|den|) at most, one step per distinct remainder

solutions.title: Long division with a remainder map
solutions.idea: Record where each remainder first produced a digit; the first remainder that comes back marks the start of the repeating block.

solutions.title: Count the non-repeating digits first
solutions.idea: After reducing the fraction, the digits before the repeat come from the factors 2 and 5 of the denominator. Emit that many digits, remember the remainder, and keep going until it returns.

followups: Go the other way: turn "0.58(3)" back into a reduced fraction.
How long can the repeating block be for a given denominator, and what decides it?
